title: The pot that died
hookLine: a borrowed pot "gives birth," later "dies," and the neighbor who believed the first can't refuse the second (Nasruddin tale)

cards: You lend a neighbor your big cooking pot, the one for soup for twenty. A few days later there's a knock: your neighbor, holding your pot, and inside it, a tiny little pot. Congratulations, he says.
While your pot was with me, it gave birth. This one's yours too. What do you do?
You know pots don't give birth. But it's a free pot, and your neighbor is smiling. That neighbor is Nasruddin, and in Turkey this story lives on in a saying: the cauldron gave birth.

teach.b: The neighbor takes the little pot. Of course he does. He doesn't argue with the miracle; he thanks Nasruddin and goes home happy.
A few weeks later, Nasruddin knocks again. Could he borrow the big pot one more time? Gladly.
Days pass. A week. No pot.
Finally the neighbor goes over to ask for it back, and Nasruddin puts on a long, sad face. I'm so sorry. Your pot has died.
Died? Don't be ridiculous. A pot can't die!
And Nasruddin answers: you believed it could give birth. Why can't you believe it could die? The trap closes perfectly.
The neighbor never believed the pot gave birth.
He believed the free pot. The story was nonsense in his favor, so he let it pass, and the moment the same nonsense cost him something, he found his good sense again.
Psychologists have a name for this: motivated reasoning.

teach.h: WE WAVE THROUGH WHAT WE LIKE.
teach.b: We check hard the claims we don't like, and wave through the claims we do: a compliment we'd love to be true, a shortcut that probably isn't allowed, a story about why the mess isn't our fault.

teach.h: WOULD I ACCEPT IT IF IT COST ME?
teach.b: Nasruddin's trick has a fairness to it.

teach.h: IF IT CAN GIVE BIRTH, IT CAN DIE.
teach.b: He never asks the neighbor to swallow a new kind of nonsense. He serves the same nonsense a second time, and holds the two halves side by side.
The test he leaves is a simple one: before you accept a pleasant claim, ask, would I accept this if it cost me?

how: Nasruddin's pot story is told across Turkey, Iran and Central Asia, and in Turkish the phrase "the cauldron gave birth" is still used, half joking, for a claim too good to be true.

games.q: you're the neighbor. Nasruddin hands back your big pot with a small one inside: congratulations, it gave birth. what do you do?
o: laugh and hand back the little pot.
thank him and take the little pot home.
ask where he really got it.
games.why: he takes it, happily, and so the trap is set. when the big pot later dies, he can't refuse a story he already accepted.

practice: Think of something you believe that happens to suit you very well: that the rule doesn't really apply here, that you're too busy for that call, that someone else will handle it.
Without arguing, ask it gently: would I believe you if you cost me something? Notice what happens in your chest, and just see the little pot for what it is.
